ukmt-cayley-2019-c1.title: Two equations
ukmt-cayley-2019-c1.body:
Let Alice be $a$ and Beatrice $b$ years old now.

In 8 years: $a+8=2(b+8)$, i.e. $a-2b=8$. (1)

Ten years ago: $(a-10)+(b-10)=21$, i.e. $a+b=41$. (2)

Add (1) to $2\times$(2): $3a=90$, so $a=30$. (Then $b=11$; check: $38=2\cdot19$ and $20+1=21$.)

**Answer: 30**

ukmt-cayley-2019-c2.title: Column by column
ukmt-cayley-2019-c2.body:
Two different digits add to between $0+1=1$ and $8+9=17$.

- Units: $G+T$ ends in $0$ and lies between $1$ and $17$, so $G+T=10$, with a carry of $1$.
- Tens: $O+A+1$ ends in $0$, so $O+A+1=10$, i.e. $O+A=9$, with a carry of $1$.
- Hundreds: $D+C+1=10$, i.e. $D+C=9$ (and the carry makes the thousands digit $1$).

Adding the three equations: $D+O+G+C+A+T=9+9+10=28$.

This is attainable, for example $124+876=1000$, where $D,O,G,C,A,T=1,2,4,8,7,6$ are six different digits.

**Answer: 28**

ukmt-cayley-2019-c3.title: Chase angles
ukmt-cayley-2019-c3.body:
Let $\angle ABC=x^\circ$.

- $BD=AD$, so triangle $ABD$ is isosceles and $\angle DAB=\angle ABD=x^\circ$.
- The exterior angle of triangle $ABD$ at $D$ is $\angle ADC=x+x=2x^\circ$.
- $AC=AD$, so $\angle ACD=\angle ADC=2x^\circ$, i.e. $\angle BCA=2x^\circ$.
- $AB=BC$, so $\angle CAB=\angle BCA=2x^\circ$.

Angle sum in triangle $ABC$: $x+2x+2x=180$, so $x=36$.

**Answer: $36^\circ$**

ukmt-cayley-2019-c4.title: Compare thousands digits, then the tails
ukmt-cayley-2019-c4.body:
Let the numbers be $P<Q$, with thousands digits $a$ and $e$ and three-digit tails $p$ and $q$ (so $P=1000a+p$, $Q=1000e+q$). All eight digits are different, so $e\ne a$ and $e>a$.

If $e\ge a+2$ then $Q-P>1000$ (since $p<1000$ and $q\ge0$: $Q-P\ge 2000+q-p>1000$). We expect a much smaller difference, so take $e=a+1$:
$$Q-P=1000+q-p .$$
We want $q$ as small and $p$ as large as possible. The tail $q$ uses three different digits from $1$-$8$, so $q\ge123$; the tail $p$ uses three different digits, so $p\le 876$. Hence
$$Q-P\ge1000+123-876=247 .$$
Equality needs $q=123$, $p=876$, which leaves the digits $4$ and $5$ for $a$ and $e$, and indeed $e=a+1$ works with $a=4$, $e=5$:
$$5123-4876=247 .$$
(Any arrangement with $e\ge a+2$ gives more than $1000$, which is bigger than $247$.)

**Answer: 247** (from $5123-4876$)

ukmt-cayley-2019-c5.title: Forbidden pairs
ukmt-cayley-2019-c5.body:
Two different numbers from the list add to between $2+3=5$ and $10+11=21$, so the only squares that can occur are $9$ and $16$. The forbidden pairs are
$$\{2,7\},\{3,6\},\{4,5\}\ (\text{sum }9),\qquad \{5,11\},\{6,10\},\{7,9\}\ (\text{sum }16).$$

**Upper bound.** The three pairs $\{2,7\},\{3,6\},\{4,5\}$ are disjoint, and Howard may take at most one number from each, so at most $3$ of these six numbers; the remaining four numbers $8,9,10,11$ give at most $4$. Hence $n\le 3+4=7$.

**Construction.** Take $2,3,4,8,9,10,11$. None of the six forbidden pairs is contained in this set (each contains one of $5,6,7$), so no two numbers add to a square.

**Answer: 7**

ukmt-cayley-2019-c6.title: Chords between lattice points, then a turning-angle argument
ukmt-cayley-2019-c6.body:
Put the board on the grid $[0,8]^2$ and let the white squares be those $[i,i+1]\times[j,j+1]$ with $i+j$ odd (the other colouring is a reflection). A closed unit square has diameter $\sqrt2$.

**Setting up.** The circle may leave a white square only through a corner, since the squares sharing an edge with a white square are black. Let the circle have radius $r>\frac{\sqrt2}{2}$ (we show later that smaller circles are no better). Call the corners it passes through *corner points*.

- It has at least $3$ corner points. With none, it lies in one white square; with one or two, some arc between consecutive corner points would be at least a semicircle (and lie in one white square), but such an arc has diameter $2r>\sqrt2$, which cannot fit in a unit square.
- Two consecutive corner points $Y,X$ are joined by an arc inside one white square, so $YX$ is a side (length $1$) or a diagonal (length $\sqrt2$) of that square.
- At a corner point $Y$, the arcs on its two sides lie in the two white squares at $Y$, which are diagonally opposite. (If both lay in the same square, the circle would pass through three corners of that square, forcing $r=\frac{\sqrt2}{2}$.)

**Consecutive chords differ in length.** Let $X,Y,Z$ be consecutive corner points. If $XY$ and $YZ$ are both diagonals, they lie along the same line (the diagonals of the two opposite white squares through $Y$ are collinear), so three points of the circle would be collinear, impossible. If both are sides, then $X,Y,Z$ are either collinear (impossible) or form a right angle at $Y$, making $XZ$ a diameter of length $\sqrt2$ and $r=\frac{\sqrt2}{2}$, excluded. So side-chords and diagonal-chords alternate around the circle.

**The radius is forced.** A side-chord has a horizontal or vertical direction and a diagonal-chord has direction at $45^\circ$ to it, so the direction turns by an odd multiple of $45^\circ$ from one chord to the next. For an inscribed polygon the turn between consecutive chords is half the sum of their central angles, i.e. $\alpha+\beta$ where $\alpha=\arcsin\frac1{2r}$ and $\beta=\arcsin\frac{\sqrt2}{2r}$; here $0<\alpha+\beta<135^\circ$, so $\alpha+\beta=45^\circ$. Then $\sin\beta=\sqrt2\sin\alpha$ gives $\frac{\sqrt2}2(\cos\alpha-\sin\alpha)=\sqrt2\sin\alpha$, so $\tan\alpha=\frac13$, $\sin\alpha=\frac1{\sqrt{10}}$ and
$$r=\frac{\sqrt{10}}{2}.$$
Every admissible circle with $r>\frac{\sqrt2}2$ therefore has this radius, and circles with $r\le\frac{\sqrt2}{2}$ are smaller. So the radius cannot exceed $\frac{\sqrt{10}}2$.

**It is attained.** Take the centre $(2.5,\,3.5)$ and radius $\frac{\sqrt{10}}{2}$. The circle passes through the eight corner points $(1,3),(1,4),(2,5),(3,5),(4,4),(4,3),(3,2),(2,2)$, and each arc between consecutive ones lies in one of the squares $[0,1]\times[3,4]$, $[1,2]\times[4,5]$, $[2,3]\times[5,6]$, $[3,4]\times[4,5]$, $[4,5]\times[3,4]$, $[3,4]\times[2,3]$, $[2,3]\times[1,2]$, $[1,2]\times[2,3]$, all of which have $i+j$ odd, i.e. are white.

**Answer: $\dfrac{\sqrt{10}}{2}$ cm**
